Cottonization.deeper: Bast technical fibers are bundles of elementary cells bound by pectin and hemicellulose, and long hemp bast is reported at about 55 to 72 percent cellulose with about 2 to 5 percent lignin. Cottonization breaks those bundles into finer units, removes residual woody shive and cuts the fiber to lengths that short-staple cotton machinery can draft, using mechanical opening and, in some routes, chemical or enzymatic degumming. The target is set by cotton itself: upland cotton staple typically runs about 7/8 to 1 5/16 inches. The alternative is the long-fiber route, and a 2018 study that scutched and hackled hemp on flax machinery found yellow-stem varieties scutched more efficiently and controlled dew retting gave a higher yield of hackled fiber than bio-degumming. In cottonized blends the hemp share is hard to confirm by eye, so percentage claims depend on documentation and quantitative analysis.
Cottonization.origins: The word describes a purpose: making bast fiber behave enough like cotton to run on the cotton spinning system. Interest revived as hemp regained legal status. In the United States, the Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018 defines hemp as Cannabis sativa L. with not more than 0.3 percent delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol on a dry weight basis (7 U.S.C. 1639o), and since 1 January 2023 the EU farm framework supports approved varieties up to 0.3 percent. Growth in cultivation brought renewed demand for decortication and cottonizing lines.

Dehairing.deeper: Dehairing works because down and guard hair differ in diameter, stiffness, length and mass. In one study of Changthangi goats, down averaged about 13 microns and 48 mm long while guard hair averaged about 68 microns and 81 mm; in coarser Bakerwal and Kargil goats guard hair exceeded 100 microns. Fleece composition varies too: Raeini cashmere goats in Iran averaged about 66 percent cashmere and 34 percent guard hair. Machines exploit these contrasts with repeated opening and carding-type actions in which heavier, stiffer hairs are thrown out while fine down is carried forward, and several passes may be needed. The US statutory test shows what counts as success: a cashmere product must have a mean diameter not over 19 microns, a coefficient of variation not over 24 percent and no more than 3 percent by weight of fibers over 30 microns.
Dehairing.origins: Kashmir shawls woven from fine goat down were luxury goods in Mughal and later courts, and nineteenth-century European mills copied their buta motif so extensively that it took the name of Paisley. European industry then shifted from importing finished shawls to importing raw down, and Bradford firms such as Joseph Dawson Ltd of Cashmere Works industrialized mechanical dehairing in the late nineteenth century. A 1996 review noted that the absence of acceptable small-scale dehairing equipment limited cottage-scale cashmere processing in the United States.

Denier.deeper: Because denier is mass per 9,000 meters, conversion to the other linear-density units is a fixed ratio: tex (grams per 1,000 m) equals denier divided by 9, and decitex (grams per 10,000 m) equals denier divided by 0.9, so 1 denier is about 1.11 dtex. For diameter, the polymer density is also needed: for a solid round filament, mass per length equals density times cross-sectional area, so in cgs units d (cm) = sqrt(4 x denier / (pi x density x 900,000)), since 9,000 m is 900,000 cm. With d in micrometers and density in g/cm3 this becomes denier = 0.00707 x d squared x density, or d = 11.89 x sqrt(denier / density). A 15 micrometer polypropylene filament (density about 0.89 g/cm3) therefore works out to roughly 1.4 denier. Hollow or non-round sections need the measured cross-sectional area instead.
Denier.origins: The unit borrows the name of a coin. English denier comes through French from Latin denarius, a Roman coin whose name derives from deni, 'ten each'. A Frankish silver denier was first issued in the late seventh century, and in France the denier survived as one twelfth of a sou until it was withdrawn in the 19th century. Silk was traditionally weighed against this small coin, and the modern definition fixes the practice as 1 gram per 9,000 meters, a length at which a single silk strand weighs roughly one gram.

Drape.deeper: Drape is usually quantified with a drapemeter. A circular specimen is centered on a smaller horizontal disk and allowed to fall into folds, and light from below casts its projected outline. The drape coefficient is (shadow area minus disk area) divided by (specimen area minus disk area), times 100. A fabric that stayed perfectly flat would score 100 percent and one hanging straight down would approach 0, so lower values indicate a more fluid drape. The original technique traced the shadow onto a paper ring, then cut out and weighed the shadow portion, using paper mass as a proxy for area; image analysis now performs the same measurement, for example in ISO 9073-9 for nonwovens. Drape coefficient can be interpreted alongside bending rigidity from the cantilever method of ASTM D1388 and the bending and shear values measured by KES-F.
Drape.origins: Quantitative drape work rests on bending studies. Peirce's 1930 cantilever test estimated bending stiffness from the overhanging length of a fabric strip and the angle its free end drops under its own weight, and a modified form is the preferred method in ASTM D1388. Cusick's 1968 paper 'The measurement of fabric drape' in the Journal of the Textile Institute (volume 59) described the cut-and-weigh shadow technique, and the Cusick drapemeter became the standard way to report a drape coefficient; drape testers are still built to BS 5058 and ISO 9073-9.

Dyeing.deeper: Dyeing is sorption followed by diffusion and fixation, and the dye class must match the fiber's chemistry. Cellulose takes reactive, direct, vat and sulfur dyes through its hydroxyl groups; wool and silk, as amphoteric proteins, take acid, metal-complex and reactive dyes; nylon binds acid dyes at terminal amine groups; dense, hydrophobic polyester lacks ionic sites and needs disperse dyes at high temperature or with carriers. Reactive dyes form covalent bonds with cellulose, but hydroxide in the bath competes with the fiber, so fixation stays below 100 percent and effluent carries unreacted dye and salt. On wool, the cuticle is the first barrier: quantitative descriptors of scale morphology correlate with the diffusion coefficient of acid dye. Dyeing can happen as loose stock, top, yarn, fabric or garment; solution dyeing bypasses the bath by adding pigment to the spinning dope.
Dyeing.origins: Mordant dyeing is ancient: brazilwood-type red dyes were recorded in Asia by the second century BC and bonded to cloth with metallic mordants. Indigo, a vat dye, was long obtained from Indigofera plants, and the class name refers to the vessel in which the reduced dyebath was prepared. New fibers forced new chemistry: cellulose acetate would not take cotton dyes, and around 1923 British Celanese and the British Dyestuffs Corporation independently developed fine aqueous dispersions of sparingly soluble dyes, the origin of the disperse class later essential for polyester.
